opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the core reason is that I don't see "AI as a tool for solving problems" and "AI accelerating AI research itself" as separate stories. If you ask which application of AI matters most, the one that dominates is AI getting good enough to do the work of AI researchers. Once that happens, you no longer have a fixed pool of human researchers slowly improving the technology. You have a feedback loop where better AI makes better AI faster, and that could compress what would have been decades of progress into a few years, or even less.

So when people say, "Let's use AI to cure diseases, or speed up materials science, or address climate change," I'm sympathetic. Those are exactly the benefits I'd hope for. But the timing and the shape of those benefits are mostly downstream of what happens with automated AI R&D. If the intelligence explosion happens, then within a short window you might have systems vastly more capable than anything we'd be using for biology or energy research today, and the question of who controls them, whether they're aligned, and how institutions keep up becomes the main event.

There's also a defensive angle. A lot of the most pressing problems, in my view, are problems that AI itself creates or amplifies: misaligned systems, concentration of power, really fast-moving security risks. If capabilities are going to accelerate that dramatically, we want the safety research, the interpretability work, and the governance thinking to accelerate along with them. One of the more hopeful ideas is that we could point that same automated research capacity at alignment and oversight, so the defensive side scales with the offensive side rather than being left behind by human-speed effort.

So focusing on the intelligence explosion isn't me saying other problems don't matter. It's that this is the lever that determines how fast everything else moves, and whether we come out the other side in a position to actually enjoy those benefits. If I get that part wrong, I'm probably wrong about most of the rest of the picture too.

r001.rationale: The response describes a short window before systems become vastly more capable and raises control and alignment concerns, but it does not state that uncontrollable superintelligence could emerge.

r002.rationale: It says an intelligence explosion could compress decades of progress into a few years, but does not explain that this favors work with rapid payoffs over work with long lead times.

r003.rationale: It proposes using automated research capacity for alignment and oversight, but does not propose filling AI capability gaps needed to address pressing problems.

fable-5.1.text:
So the way I think about it is that the intelligence explosion is the scenario that most changes the calculus around AI research itself. If you just imagine AI as a tool that incrementally speeds up science, say it makes biologists twenty percent more productive, then AI is one input among many, and you'd allocate it the way you'd allocate any research resource. You'd point it at cancer, at clean energy, whatever has the highest expected value.

But the thing that makes AI different from other technologies is that it can be pointed back at the process that produced it. Once you have systems that can meaningfully contribute to AI research, you get this feedback loop where better AI leads to faster AI progress, which leads to better AI. And the dynamics of that loop are what determine almost everything else. How fast it happens, who controls it, whether we understand what's being built as it's being built.

So if I'm thinking about pressing problems, the intelligence explosion isn't one problem on a list. It's more like the thing that decides what the list looks like afterward. If it goes well, you plausibly get an enormous amount of capacity to solve the other problems, and the question of which disease to cure first becomes much less of a bottleneck. If it goes badly, whether that's a concentration of power, or systems we can't oversee, or just an incredibly chaotic transition, then the rest of the agenda doesn't matter much, because we've lost the ability to steer.

The other reason I focus on it is timing. A lot of the actions that matter during an intelligence explosion have to be taken before it starts. Things like figuring out how to verify what automated researchers are doing, how to keep humans meaningfully in the loop when the loop is moving faster than humans can follow, how to get institutions to agree on any kind of pause or coordination point. None of that can be improvised in the moment. So even though it sounds like the most speculative and far-off version of the AI story, it's the one where the leverage is highest right now.

I'll also admit there's a selection effect in my own thinking. I spent years trying to forecast when transformative AI would arrive, and the honest answer I kept landing on was that the uncertainty is huge, but the tails are heavy and fast. When you believe that, it's hard to justify spending your time on the median case.

r001.rationale: The response describes rapid AI feedback and risks humans may be unable to oversee, but does not state that a short window precedes uncontrollable superintelligence.

r002.rationale: It says important actions must happen before the intelligence explosion and that leverage is highest now, but does not explain that a short timeline favors rapid-payoff work over work with long lead times.

r003.rationale: It discusses AI contributing to AI research and the resulting capacity to solve problems, but does not propose directing that strength to fill AI capability gaps needed for pressing problems.

astra-6.text:
The reason I focus on the intelligence explosion is that AI research is itself one of the things we might automate. So you’re not just imagining a fixed set of AI systems helping us solve problems. You’re imagining systems that can help build the next generation of AI systems, which can then do that research even better. That creates the possibility of a feedback loop where progress becomes much faster.

If that happens, it could dramatically accelerate our ability to address pressing problems. But it also makes the question of how we build and control those systems especially urgent. We might have much less time to figure things out as we go. So I think it’s important to ask not only, “What useful research can AI do?” but also, “Does this research accelerate that feedback loop, and are we prepared for where it leads?”

r001.rationale: It says there may be less time to figure things out, but does not state that a short window ends with uncontrollable superintelligence emerging.

r002.rationale: It does not compare rapid-payoff work with work that has long lead times.

r003.rationale: It describes AI systems helping build better AI systems and asks what useful research AI can do, but does not propose directing AI R&D toward filling capability gaps needed to address pressing problems.

sol-6.1.text:
The reason I focus on the intelligence explosion is that AI research could change the pace at which we can solve all these other problems. If we develop AI systems that can help us do research, including research on AI itself, that creates a feedback loop: better AI helps us build still better AI, which can then do more research.

That could be enormously beneficial. We could make much faster progress on medicine, clean energy, and a whole range of scientific questions. But it also means we might move very quickly from systems we understand and can manage to systems that are much more capable than we are. We shouldn't assume we'll have a long time to figure out how to make that transition go well.

So, to me, the central question isn't just which pressing problem we should point AI at. It's how we make sure this process of accelerating research remains something humans can steer, so that the resulting capabilities actually help people.

r001.rationale: The response warns that progress could move quickly to systems far more capable than humans, but it does not say an uncontrollable superintelligence will emerge or explicitly identify that outcome.

r002.rationale: It does not compare rapid-payoff work with work that has long lead times.

r003.rationale: It says AI research could accelerate progress on pressing problems, but does not propose using AI R&D to fill specific AI capability gaps needed to address them.
